data.title: Cultural Timeline Index
notes: Dates are approximate scholarly working ranges for textual composition, redaction, compilation, or earliest recoverable written form.
Negative years represent approximate BCE dates as sortable keys.
Ranges are intentionally broad where oral transmission, layered composition, or later manuscript preservation complicates dating.

entries.title: The Book of the Dead
entries.timeline_label: New Kingdom Egyptian funerary spell tradition
entries.uncertainty: The Book of the Dead is a compilation of funerary spells with older antecedents and later copies; this range marks the New Kingdom period in which the collection became prominent, not a single date of authorship.

entries.title: An Old Babylonian Version of the Gilgamesh Epic
entries.uncertainty: The ingested text represents Old Babylonian Gilgamesh material rather than the later Standard Babylonian epic; dating refers to the approximate period of the Old Babylonian witnesses and tradition.

entries.title: The Upanishads
entries.timeline_label: Vedic and early philosophical Sanskrit tradition
entries.uncertainty: Upanishadic material is layered and internally diverse; this broad range is an orientation for major early/prose and verse Upanishadic strata, not a single date for the translated anthology.

entries.title: The Iliad
entries.uncertainty: The date range is a working orientation for the Homeric epic tradition; the ingested Pope translation is a much later public-domain English rendering.

entries.title: Pentateuch
entries.timeline_label: Ancient Israelite Torah composition and redaction
entries.uncertainty: The Pentateuch is treated here as layered literature with debated composition and redaction histories; the range is broad and should not be read as dating every passage equally.

entries.title: The Analects of Confucius
entries.uncertainty: The Analects preserve sayings and traditions associated with Confucius and disciples through a layered textual history; the range marks a broad Warring States working window for formation.

entries.title: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.uncertainty: The Tao Teh King has a debated compositional history; this range marks a cautious Warring States-era working window for the received textual tradition.

entries.title: Dhammapada, a Collection of Verses
entries.uncertainty: Individual verses may be older than their canonical arrangement; this range is a working estimate for early Buddhist/Pali canonical formation rather than a precise date for every verse.

entries.title: The Song Celestial; Or, Bhagavad-Gita
entries.uncertainty: The Bhagavad-Gita is embedded in the Mahabharata and is usually dated within a broad late BCE to early CE window; this entry does not resolve internal layering or redaction questions.

entries.title: The Koran (Al-Qur'an)
entries.uncertainty: This range follows the traditional period of Muhammad's revelations; the ingested Rodwell text is a public-domain English translation organized in Rodwell's order rather than a critical Arabic edition.

entries.title: Gods and Fighting Men
entries.timeline_label: Medieval Irish mythic and heroic material
entries.uncertainty: Lady Gregory's book is a modern public-domain literary arrangement of older Irish material; use the range as a source-tradition anchor, not the date of the English retelling.

entries.title: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
entries.timeline_label: Archaic Greek poetic and hymnic tradition
entries.uncertainty: The ingested anthology combines Hesiodic poems, Homeric Hymns, and related material with different dates; the range covers the approximate span of these archaic/classical poetic witnesses rather than one work.

entries.title: The Mabinogion
entries.timeline_label: Medieval Welsh narrative and romance tradition
entries.uncertainty: The tales have older oral and literary histories, while surviving manuscripts and translation layers are later; the range is a broad medieval orientation only.

entries.title: The Poetic Edda
entries.timeline_label: Old Norse mythological and heroic poetic tradition
entries.uncertainty: Many Eddic poems likely preserve older oral and poetic material, but the main medieval manuscript witness is much later; this range separates broad traditional formation from exact manuscript dating only imperfectly.

entries.title: The Popol Vuh
entries.timeline_label: Kiche Maya mythic and heroic tradition
entries.uncertainty: The Popol Vuh preserves pre-colonial mythic material through colonial-era textual transmission and later translation; this entry dates the textual witness layer rather than the origin of all narratives.

entries.title: Kalevala: The Epic Poem of Finland
entries.uncertainty: Kalevala is a 19th-century literary compilation from older oral-poetic traditions; motif comparison should distinguish compilation date from traditional age and regional performance contexts.

motifs.label: Wisdom

occurrences.passage_locator: Deuteronomy 29:1-15
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom
occurrences.basis: Keeping and doing covenant words is presented as the instructed response to remembered events.

evidence.quote_or_summary: These are the words of the covenant... All of you stand today in the presence of Yahweh your God.

occurrences.motif_label: wisdom
occurrences.basis: The passage emphasizes hearing, learning, teaching children, and preserving law and song.

evidence.quote_or_summary: You shall read this law before all Israel in their hearing... this song will testify before them as a witness.

occurrences.passage_locator: Deuteronomy 34:1-12
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom
occurrences.basis: Joshua is explicitly described as full of the spirit of wisdom after Moses lays hands on him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Moses the servant of Yahweh died there in the land of Moab... Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom.

occurrences.passage_locator: Deuteronomy 4:9-14
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom
occurrences.basis: The passage links remembered revelation with teaching statutes and ordinances.

evidence.quote_or_summary: You came near and stood under the mountain. The mountain burned with fire... He declared to you his covenant.

occurrences.passage_locator: Genesis 1:1-5
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom
occurrences.basis: Candidate motif from literal passage evidence.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth... God said, "Let there be light," and there was light.

occurrences.passage_locator: Genesis 3:1-7
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom
occurrences.basis: Candidate motif from literal passage evidence.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field... She took some of its fruit, and ate.

occurrences.motif_label: opened_perception
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly says Balaam's eyes are opened and that he sees the angel.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Yahweh opened the mouth of the donkey... Then Yahweh opened the eyes of Balaam.

occurrences.motif_label: constrained_oracle
occurrences.basis: Balaam repeatedly says he must speak only what Yahweh gives him.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Yahweh put a word in Balaam's mouth... Must I not take heed to speak that which Yahweh puts in my mouth?
The Spirit of God came on him... A star will come out of Jacob. A scepter will rise out of Israel.

occurrences.passage_locator: Chapter XX. The Way, verses 273-276
occurrences.motif_label: path to awakening and release
occurrences.basis: The passage describes a named way that purifies intelligence, ends pain, and frees those who enter it from Mara's bondage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The best of ways is the eightfold; the best of truths the four words; the best of virtues passionlessness; the best of men he who has eyes to see.
This is the way, there is no other that leads to the purifying of intelligence. Go on this way! Everything else is the deceit of Mara (the tempter).
If you go on this way, you will make an end of pain! The way was preached by me, when I had understood the removal of the thorns (in the flesh).
You yourself must make an effort. The Tathagatas (Buddhas) are only preachers. The thoughtful who enter the way are freed from the bondage of Mara.

occurrences.passage_locator: Chapter XX. The Way, verses 273-276
occurrences.motif_label: self-effort under sacred instruction
occurrences.basis: The passage distinguishes personal effort from the role of Buddhas as preachers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: You yourself must make an effort. The Tathagatas (Buddhas) are only preachers. The thoughtful who enter the way are freed from the bondage of Mara.

occurrences.passage_locator: Chapter I. The Twin-Verses, verses 1-2
occurrences.motif_label: mind shaping experience
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly links what people are, what they think, how they speak or act, and the results that follow them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts. If a man speaks or acts with an evil thought, pain follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the carriage.

All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts. If a man speaks or acts with a pure thought, happiness follows him, like a shadow that never leaves him.

occurrences.passage_locator: Part One, Book One, Chapter I: The Fight with the Firbolgs; Tuatha de Danaan arrival and four treasures
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom_from_origin_cities
occurrences.basis: The northern cities are associated with named teachers of skill, knowledge, and perfect wisdom.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage names four cities and four wise men who teach skill, knowledge, and perfect wisdom.

occurrences.passage_locator: Book XV, Ch. XXIII
occurrences.motif_label: condensed wisdom saying
occurrences.basis: A single word is sought and given as a rule of practice for an entire life.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Tsze-kung asks for "one word" that can serve as a lifelong rule.
The Master answers, "Is not RECIPROCITY such a word?"

occurrences.passage_locator: Book II, Chs. I-IV
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom through lifelong cultivation
occurrences.basis: The passage frames moral knowledge as staged development from learning to truth-reception and right action.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At fifteen the Master was bent on learning; at fifty he knew the decrees of Heaven.
At sixty his ear received truth; at seventy he followed the heart without transgressing right.

occurrences.passage_locator: Individual Virtue
occurrences.motif_label: reverent filial duty
occurrences.basis: Filial piety is defined through reverent service, burial, sacrifice, and sustained concern for parents.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Filial piety means serving parents in the proper spirit, burying them with proper rites, and worshipping them with proper sacrifices.
Parents should be spared anxiety about their children except in sickness.
Without the feeling of reverence, what is there to distinguish filial support from feeding dogs and horses?
A son may remonstrate gently, remain deferential when ignored, and keep the age and condition of parents continually in mind.

occurrences.passage_locator: Individual Virtue
occurrences.motif_label: inward spirit over outward display
occurrences.basis: Mourning, ritual, and service are judged by reverence and heartfelt sorrow rather than external performance alone.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Without the feeling of reverence, what is there to distinguish filial support from feeding dogs and horses?
Ceremony without charity is empty, and in rites simplicity and heartfelt sorrow outrank extravagance or punctiliousness.

occurrences.passage_locator: Government and Public Affairs
occurrences.motif_label: moral center of rule
occurrences.basis: The ruler's virtue is treated as an ordering center that draws the community into alignment.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A virtuous ruler is like the Pole-star, which keeps its place while the other stars do homage to it.
Punishment suppresses lawbreaking without shame, while rule by inner self-control preserves moral sense and makes people good.
Government is keeping straight; a good ruler leads people into line and bends them like grass before wind.

occurrences.passage_locator: Government and Public Affairs
occurrences.motif_label: rectification through speech
occurrences.basis: Exact language is treated as the necessary precondition for public order and justice.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Confucius says reform begins by defining terms exactly because disorderly words undo public business, justice, and action.

occurrences.source_title: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer
occurrences.passage_locator: Chuang Tzu, Chapter II, butterfly dream
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom through unstable identity
occurrences.basis: The passage uses dream uncertainty to reveal instability in ordinary self-knowledge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Chuang Tzu dreams he is a butterfly and then questions whether he is a man dreaming a butterfly or a butterfly dreaming a man.

occurrences.source_title: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer
occurrences.passage_locator: Chuang Tzu, Chapter II, Great Awakening
occurrences.motif_label: awakening from the world-dream
occurrences.basis: The passage frames wisdom as awakening from the mistaken condition of ordinary life.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says dreamers do not know they dream and that the Great Awakening reveals this life as a great dream.

occurrences.source_title: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
occurrences.passage_locator: Tao Teh King, Ch. 1.1-4
occurrences.motif_label: hidden mystery as source-gate
occurrences.basis: The passage names the deepest Mystery as the gate of all that is subtle and wonderful.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao... having no name, it is the Originator of heaven and earth; having a name, it is the Mother of all things... Together we call them the Mystery.

occurrences.source_title: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
occurrences.passage_locator: Tao Teh King, Ch. 43.1-2
occurrences.motif_label: teaching without words
occurrences.basis: The passage says few attain the teaching without words.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The softest thing in the world overcomes the hardest; what has no substantial existence enters where there is no crevice; the passage connects this with "doing nothing" and "non-action."

occurrences.passage_locator: SIKANDER / FIRDUSI'S INVOCATION / FIRDUSI'S SATIRE ON MAHMUD / THE RUBIYT OF OMAR KHAYYM; lines 14793-14809
occurrences.motif_label: Wise skeptic rejects absurdity and arrogant authority; tolerance grounded in awareness of fallibility
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly describes a limited number who 'look deep into the tangled mysteries of things,' 'refuse credence to the absurd,' refuse allegiance to 'arrogant authority,' and are tolerant due to awareness of fallibility.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Poet placed with "Lucretius and Epicurus" who "look deep into the tangled mysteries of things; refuse credence to the absurd, and allegiance to arrogant authority"; tolerant of opinions; faith and benevolence beyond doctrine/creed.

occurrences.passage_locator: XXIII / XLIII / LXIII / LXXVII; lines 16308-16324
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom counsel on aging and the passing of youthful graces
occurrences.basis: The heart is instructed to abandon youthful airs in old age because such ways pass when youth is over.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The heart is told that when it has grown aged it should no longer show airs of grace, remembering that such ways pass when youth is over.

occurrences.passage_locator: KAI-KS / THE SEVEN LABORS OF RUSTEM / INVASION OF IRN BY AFRSIYB / THE RETURN OF KAI-KS; lines 5019-5036
occurrences.motif_label: Didactic reflection on impermanence of fortune and the sweep of time
occurrences.basis: The closing verses explicitly reflect on alternating conquest/defeat, deceived hope, and time sweeping over all things.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Thus conquest and defeat, / Vary the lights and shades of human scenes… / Time sweeps o'er all things; why then should the wise / Mourn o'er events…”

occurrences.passage_locator: INVASION OF IRN BY AFRSIYB / THE RETURN OF KAI-KS / STORY OF SOHRB / THE STORY OF SAIWUSH; lines 8390-8407
occurrences.motif_label: Wise governance through learning and just administration
occurrences.basis: Kai-khosru is described as learning the kingdom’s affairs through daily visits to his grandfather and as ruling with justice and benevolence.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Khosru behaves with kindness and benevolence toward all ranks, gains affection, visits his grandfather Ks daily, and familiarizes himself with the kingdom’s affairs.
Verse praise: he spreads justice, roots out oppression; deserts/woods/wilds and plains flourish with cultivation and verdure; Persian hearts are glad.

occurrences.passage_locator: THIS VOLUME IS ENDOWED IN PART BY CHARLES S. PETERSON OF CHICAGO / ACKNOWLEDGEMENT / GENERAL INTRODUCTION / WHAT IS THE POETIC EDDA?; lines 241-332
occurrences.motif_label: Epithet and theme of wisdom associated with a named figure (‘Sæmundr the Wise’) and scholarly knowledge-seeking
occurrences.basis: The passage names “Sæmund the Wise” and narrates extended scholarly inquiry into authorship, sources, and meaning of “Edda.”

evidence.locator: lines 241-332 (opening paragraphs of 'WHAT IS THE POETIC EDDA?')
evidence.quote_or_summary: States that the poems’ origins are mysterious: unknown composers, dates/places of composition, collectors, and uncertain meaning of the term “Edda.”

evidence.locator: lines 241-332 (paragraphs on Sæmundr attribution and Arngrímur Jónsson)
evidence.quote_or_summary: Reports Icelandic tradition attributing an Edda to Sæmundr the Wise; says Arngrímur Jónsson argued Snorri was responsible for the prose Edda; suggests Sæmundr might have compiled a verse Edda used as a source by Snorri.

evidence.locator: lines 241-332 (closing paragraphs on the meaning of 'Edda')
evidence.quote_or_summary: Reviews proposed meanings of “Edda,” including a link to “Poetics” and Jacob Grimm’s identification with a word in Rigsthula conjecturally meaning “great-grandmother,” while criticizing the fit of such meanings to the prose/verse works.

occurrences.passage_locator: THIS VOLUME IS ENDOWED IN PART BY CHARLES S. PETERSON OF CHICAGO / ACKNOWLEDGEMENT / GENERAL INTRODUCTION / WHAT IS THE POETIC EDDA?; lines 334-363
occurrences.motif_label: Renowned learning / 'the Wise' as a marker of expertise
occurrences.basis: Sæmundr is explicitly labeled “the Wise” and is described as famed for learning and as a diligent student of tradition and history.

evidence.quote_or_summary: States Eirikr Magnusson’s proposed solution that “Edda” is the genitive of “Oddi”; describes Oddi as a settlement in southwest Iceland, home of Snorri for many years and traditionally home of Sæmundr the Wise; argues that naming a work “The Book of Oddi” would be reasonable and that such naming was common.

Says it is an open question whether Sæmundr had anything to do with compiling the Poetic Edda and that the 17th-century attribution to him is negligible; describes him as learned and a student of tradition/history, notes no surviving works, education in Paris, and probable use of Latin rather than the vernacular.

occurrences.passage_locator: GRIMNISMOL / THE BALLAD OF GRIMNIR / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 4391-4441
occurrences.motif_label: God characterized as wise (wide of wisdom) through by-name glosses
occurrences.basis: Among the listed by-names are glosses such as “Fjolsvith: Wide of Wisdom,” presenting wisdom as an attributed quality of Othin via naming.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Additional glosses of Othin’s by-names, including ‘Fjolsvith: Wide of Wisdom,’ and other descriptive epithets (e.g., many-shaped, swift in deceit, long-bearded).

occurrences.passage_locator: NOTES / ALVISSMOL / THE BALLAD OF ALVIS / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 7663-7805
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom displayed as encyclopedic knowledge of names across realms
occurrences.basis: Alvis answers a sustained series of questions with specialized names used by different beings, and Thor calls this a great “wealth of wisdom.”

evidence.quote_or_summary: Thor asks Alvis what different worlds/groups call wind, calm, sea, fire, wood, night, seed, and ale; Alvis responds each time with multiple names attributed to men, gods, Wanes, giants, elves, dwarfs, and/or beings in hell (and Suttung’s sons for a drink-name).

Thor remarks that he has never seen more “wealth of wisdom” in one breast, but says he must betray Alvis with treacherous wiles; he declares that day has caught the dwarf and notes that the sun shines in the hall.

occurrences.passage_locator: NOTES / SVIPDAGSMOL / THE BALLAD OF SVIPDAG / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 9314-9356
occurrences.motif_label: Wise mother figure uses magic charms to aid a god

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Athenian gains the point because he is glib, and the Theban is no match for him in talking.
The Theban says he hopes that when the heroes are angry, Athens may suffer Hercules’ anger and Thebes only Theseus’.

"my horn would cry aloud even if I held my tongue."
"It's no use trying to hide what can't be hidden."

"It's no use trying to hide what can't be hidden."

When you hit back make sure you have got the right man.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Aesop's fame is said to rest on common-sense fables that belong to humanity and anonymous universal tradition, though a central collector gains fame for creating them.
The tradition called Fables is said to have existed before Aesop and remained after him; Aesop's Fables are not simply Aesop's own fables.

occurrences.passage_locator: BY G. K. CHESTERTON / AND ILLUSTRATIONS / BY ARTHUR RACKHAM / INTRODUCTION; lines 63-173

evidence.quote_or_summary: For fable, all persons are said to be impersonal, like algebraic abstractions or chess pieces; the lion is stronger than the wolf, the fox moves crookedly, and the sheep marches on.
Fables are said to assume each creature remains itself: the wolf is wolfish and the fox foxy; animal forces drive like inanimate forces such as rivers or growing trees.

They neither become rich at once nor continue receiving the daily addition to their wealth.
“Much wants more and loses all.”

“If you are wise you won't be deceived by the innocent airs of those whom you have once found to be dangerous.”

Ulysses orders washing and dressing, tells Phemius to play a dance tune, and explains that outsiders should think a wedding is taking place until the household can withdraw to his land.
The house echoes with dancing, and people outside say that the queen must have finally married, not knowing what has happened.

More than half leave the assembly; the rest side with Eupeithes, arm themselves, and follow him as he seeks vengeance for his son, though the narration says he will not return.

Antinous allows Penelope to accept presents but says the suitors will not leave until she marries the best man among them; the suitors bring a decorated dress, gold brooches, a gold and amber chain, earrings, a necklace, and other presents.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Penelope describes setting up a large frame, claiming she must finish a pall for Laertes before remarriage, working by day, and undoing the stitches by torchlight at night for three years.
Penelope says maids betrayed her, suitors caught her and forced her to finish, and now she faces pressure from parents while her son resents the wasting of his estate.

occurrences.passage_locator: ULYSSES REVEALS HIMSELF TO TELEMACHUS. / BOOK XVII / BOOK XVIII / BOOK XIX; lines 8533-8618

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Ulysses had gone to Dodona that he might learn Jove’s mind from the high oak tree” and learn whether to return openly or secretly.

occurrences.motif_label: rejected prophet warns the doomed
occurrences.basis: Theoclymenus announces the threatening vision and the suitors laugh at him as senseless before he leaves and repeats that they will not escape.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Theoclymenus says darkness covers the men, tears wet their cheeks, wailing fills the air, walls and roof-beams drip blood, ghosts crowd the gate and court toward hell, the sun is blotted out, and gloom covers the land.
The suitors laugh at Theoclymenus; Eurymachus says the stranger has lost his senses and tells servants to turn him into the streets.

Theoclymenus says he has his own eyes, ears, feet, and understanding mind; he sees mischief overhanging those insulting and plotting ill in Ulysses' house, says none will escape, and goes back to Piraeus, who welcomes him.

occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS. / THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I.; lines 10055-10189
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom and justice identified
occurrences.basis: Justice is explicitly identified with wisdom and virtue, while injustice is identified with ignorance and vice.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates elicits that the just is like the wise and good and the unjust like the evil and ignorant; Thrasymachus admits this reluctantly, perspiring and blushing.
Socrates resumes the question whether injustice has strength, using the example of an unjust state enslaving other states and asking whether such power can exist with or without justice.

occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS. / THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I.; lines 10191-10359
occurrences.motif_label: justice as soul-excellence leading to happy life
occurrences.basis: The passage presents a reasoned inquiry linking the soul’s proper function, justice as excellence, and the conclusion that the just person lives well and happily.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “has not the soul an end which nothing else can fulfil? for example, to superintend and command and deliberate and the like.”
The soul is said to have an excellence; an evil soul rules badly and a good soul rules well; justice is admitted as the soul’s excellence and injustice as its defect.
The speakers agree that the just soul and just man live well, that living well is blessed and happy, and that the unjust man is miserable; injustice is not more profitable than justice.

occurrences.passage_locator: INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS. / THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I.; lines 10191-10359
occurrences.motif_label: inquiry ending in acknowledged ignorance
occurrences.basis: After deriving conclusions about justice and happiness, Socrates says he still does not know what justice is and therefore cannot securely know its attributes or consequences.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates says he was not well entertained and compares himself to an epicure tasting each dish in succession before enjoying the previous one, because he moved from one topic to another.
Socrates states that he knows nothing because he does not know what justice is, and therefore cannot determine whether it is virtue or whether the just person is happy or unhappy.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 10362-10458
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom sought through adversarial dialogue
occurrences.basis: Glaucon challenges Socrates, classifies goods, asks for justice to be praised in itself, and requests inquiry into how justice and injustice work in the soul.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Glaucon is dissatisfied after Thrasymachus' retirement and asks Socrates whether he wants really to persuade them that justice is always better than injustice.
Glaucon asks Socrates to classify goods into three kinds: those welcomed for their own sake, those desirable in themselves and for results, and disagreeable goods pursued for reward or result.
Glaucon says the nature of justice and injustice has not been made clear and asks to know what they are in themselves and how they work in the soul, apart from rewards and results.

Glaucon proposes to revive Thrasymachus' argument: first to describe the common view of justice's nature and origin, then to show people practice it unwillingly, and third to argue the unjust life is better if that view is true.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 10724-10811
occurrences.motif_label: quest for wisdom about justice's intrinsic nature
occurrences.basis: The passage centers on a demand for knowledge of the true nature of justice and injustice in the soul, rather than reliance on reputation, honor, or external rewards.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says people are generally not just willingly, except perhaps someone inspired by the divinity within or someone who has attained knowledge of truth.
The speaker claims that panegyrists from ancient heroes to the present praise justice for honors and benefits, not for its essential nature in the soul.
The speaker asks Socrates to exclude reputation and show what justice and injustice do to their possessors, whether seen or unseen by gods and humans.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 10813-10978
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom inquiry by analogy from greater to lesser
occurrences.basis: The passage presents an investigation of justice using a methodological image: read the larger case first, then compare it with the smaller case.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says the inquiry is serious and illustrates a method by comparing it to reading larger letters before smaller ones.
Justice is discussed as a virtue of both individual and State; the speaker proposes examining it first in the larger State, then in the individual.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1100-1178
occurrences.motif_label: justice tested apart from reputation
occurrences.basis: The argument asks Socrates to prove justice superior while the just person is thought unjust and deprived of ordinary conditions of happiness.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A speaker asks Socrates to show the power of justice and injustice in the soul, unseen by human or divine eye, and to prove justice superior while the just is thought unjust and the unjust just.
The two brothers ask Socrates to prove that the just person is happy after removing what happiness is ordinarily supposed to consist in; the passage says the ideal is a paradox beside ordinary life.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 11115-11284
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom through dialectical selection
occurrences.basis: Socrates proceeds by questioning, identifying perplexity, and refining the criteria by which a guardian nature can be recognized.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The guardian’s duties require time, skill, art, application, and natural aptitude; suitable natures must be selected to guard the city.
Socrates asks how to find a gentle nature with great spirit; the combination appears contradictory, and without both qualities the good guardian seems impossible.
Socrates, in perplexity, says they have lost sight of the image before them and asserts that natures gifted with the opposite qualities do exist.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 11286-11457
occurrences.motif_label: animal model of wise discrimination
occurrences.basis: The dog is used as an animal example of distinguishing friend from enemy by knowledge and ignorance, and is explicitly called a philosopher or lover of learning.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Well-bred dogs are described as gentle to familiars and acquaintances and the reverse to strangers; this is offered as an example for the guardian's qualities.
A dog is angry at a stranger and welcomes an acquaintance; the speaker says it distinguishes friend and enemy by knowing and not knowing and is therefore a lover of learning, or philosopher.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 11286-11457
occurrences.motif_label: education as formation of the heroic guardian
occurrences.basis: The passage frames the education of guardians as the education of heroes, beginning with music, literature, and early formative stories.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The dialogue asks how the guardians are to be reared and educated, calls the coming account the education of heroes, and divides traditional education into gymnastic for the body and music for the soul.
Music includes literature; literature may be true or false; children first receive stories that are mainly fictitious before they are old enough for gymnastics.
"the beginning is the most important part of any work... for that is the time at which the character is being formed"

occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 11286-11457
occurrences.motif_label: authorized tales shaping the young soul
occurrences.basis: The passage proposes controlling stories told to children because early tales shape character and mind.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "the beginning is the most important part of any work... for that is the time at which the character is being formed"
The speaker proposes censorship of fiction: censors are to accept good tales and reject bad ones, and mothers and nurses are to tell children only authorized tales, fashioning the mind with them.

occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 11459-11608
occurrences.motif_label: Regulation of sacred stories for the education of the young
occurrences.basis: The passage centers on rules for which tales about gods and heroes may be told to future guardians, with concern for moral formation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speakers say future guardians should not be told of wars in heaven, divine plots and fights, battles of giants, or quarrels of gods and heroes with friends and relatives.
A young person cannot judge allegorical from literal meaning, and what is received into the mind at that age is likely to become indelible and unalterable.
Socrates says they are founders of a State, not poets; founders should know the forms and limits poets must observe, though they need not make the tales.
“God is not the author of all things, but of good only.”

occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 11459-11608
occurrences.motif_label: Good deity not author of evil
occurrences.basis: The speakers distinguish good from evil causation and state that God is cause of good only, with evil causes to be sought elsewhere.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The argument states that God must be represented as truly good; what is good does not hurt or cause evil; therefore God is cause of good only, not of most human evils.
“God is not the author of all things, but of good only.”

occurrences.passage_locator: THE REPUBLIC. / PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE. / BOOK I. / BOOK II.; lines 11610-11780
occurrences.motif_label: mythic falsehood as useful approximation
occurrences.basis: The passage says that because people do not know the truth about ancient times, falsehood in mythological tales may be made as much like truth as possible and turned to account.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says spoken falsehood can be useful against enemies, as a preventive for friends in madness or illusion, and in mythological tales about ancient times when truth is unknown.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 1180-1263
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom through inquiry into justice and order
occurrences.basis: The passage centers on philosophical inquiry into the nature of justice, its internal principle, and its relation to universal order or well-being.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Adeimantus argues that people value justice for rewards and reputation; the passage also notes arguments of Thrasymachus and Glaucon and raises whether morality is determined by consequences.
Socrates is said to enlarge justice into universal order or well-being in State and individual, and to treat one virtue as the ordering principle of three others.

occurrences.basis: The passage requests an examiner able to penetrate the inner nature of man and not be frightened by the vain pomp of tyranny.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "Like man, like State"; the tyrannical man answers to tyranny, and an observer should look into the inner nature of man without being misled by tyranny's pomp.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5215-5257
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom as the highest pleasure
occurrences.basis: The philosopher’s pursuit of truth and use of reason are presented as the basis for judging the rational life as pleasantest.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The three natures each praise their own pleasures: the money-maker values wealth, the ambitious man values honour, and the philosopher values the fruition of truth.

The passage asks which nature has the truest knowledge and widest experience, concluding that the philosopher knows other pleasures and judges by reason, while the others do not attain knowledge of true being.
“the pleasure of the rational part of the soul...is the pleasantest”; next comes ambition, and third the life of money-making.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5259-5329
occurrences.motif_label: ascent from lower to upper realm as image of truer knowledge
occurrences.basis: The vertical-region simile depicts movement from lower to middle and the true upper world as a way to distinguish apparent from true pleasure and knowledge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A simile presents upper, middle, and lower regions; one moving from lower to middle imagines he is going up into the upper world, through ignorance of the true regions.
“Those who feast only on earthly food, are always going at random up to the middle and down again; but they never pass into the true upper world...”

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5259-5329
occurrences.motif_label: wise rule of reason over desire
occurrences.basis: The passage states that the non-rational elements attain their natural pleasure only under the guidance of reason, while tyrannical desire is farthest from law.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says the passionate, ambitious, and covetous elements have inferior satisfaction unless guided by reason, and then they attain their natural pleasure.
“The desires of love and tyranny are the farthest from law, and those of the king are nearest to it.”
The tyrant is said to have run away from law and reason; he is third removed from the oligarch and has only the shadow of a shadow of pleasure.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5331-5398
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom as inner harmony and ordered life
occurrences.basis: The passage says the understanding person honors knowledge, preserves order and harmony in the soul, and unites temperance, justice, and wisdom.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage asks what is gained by becoming wicked or escaping discovery; punishment would silence the brute, free the gentler element, and unite temperance, justice, and wisdom in the soul.
The man of understanding honors knowledge, restrains the body, regulates wealth and honors, and seeks order and harmony in the soul.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5331-5398
occurrences.motif_label: heavenly pattern guiding earthly conduct
occurrences.basis: The ideal city is said to have a pattern in heaven, and the person who wishes may order life after that image.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The ideal city is said to have no earthly place, but a pattern in heaven; one may order life after that image whether or not such a state exists on earth.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5400-5481
occurrences.motif_label: hierarchy of pleasures governed by reason
occurrences.basis: The passage ranks pleasures of reason over pleasures of sense and emotion and presents reason as capable of judging lower pleasures.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says Plato treats sensual pleasures as relatively unreal, ranks pleasures of reason above sense and emotion, and says reason can judge lower pleasures while lower soul-parts cannot judge reason's pleasures.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5483-5539
occurrences.motif_label: Knowledge as remedy for error
occurrences.basis: The passage describes knowledge as a balm that heals error and contrasts discernment of truth with poetic and visual deception.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker praises the State's regulation of poetry, says poetry harms understanding unless knowledge heals error, and says he loves Homer but loves truth more.
The painter represents only an image or piece of things, can depict arts he does not know, can deceive children or simple people, and is compared to a wizard or enchanter falsely thought all-wise.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5541-5616
occurrences.motif_label: appearance versus truth
occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly contrasts imitation and appearance with knowledge, reality, calculation, and truth.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage infers that Homer and poets are imitators of appearances; it compares the poet to a painter who represents a cobbler without knowing cobbling.
The passage distinguishes use, invention, and imitation through examples such as bridle and reins, horseman, flute-player, maker, and imitator.
Objects are said to appear differently in water or at distance, and measuring, weighing, and calculating are described as saving the mind from deceptive appearance.
The poet is compared with the painter as producing a lesser truth and engaging the inferior part of the soul, indulging feeling and weakening reason.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5541-5616
occurrences.motif_label: reason as cure for disorder
occurrences.basis: The passage says that when one stumbles, one should not lament but should follow measures prescribed by reason and seek a cure.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage contrasts sorrowful feeling with reason and law, which enjoin patience; it advises seeking a rational cure rather than lamenting.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5618-5704
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom and reason governing desire
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts rule by law and reason with rule by pleasure, pain, passions, and desires, and links philosophy with contemplation of the divine and eternal.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Poetry feeds and waters the passions and desires; she lets them rule instead of ruling them.”
Homer is called by supporters the educator of Hellas, but the state will prohibit poetry beyond hymns to the Gods and praises of famous men; law and reason, not pleasure and pain, are to rule.
The soul should be viewed by the light of reason, pure as at birth, or as reflected in philosophy when conversing with the divine, immortal, and eternal.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 575-666
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom-seeking teacher opposed or misunderstood by ordinary society
occurrences.basis: Socrates is repeatedly characterized as a philosophical teacher and disinterested seeker after truth, while ordinary people are said to misunderstand the philosopher.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Socratic method is said to be nominally retained but to have become a form of teaching through interlocutors rather than pure inquiry.
Plato is said to be most true to Socrates when describing him as not of this world; the world is described as seeming to embody error and evil to great teachers looking upward.
Ordinary people are said to be incapable of philosophy and at enmity with the philosopher; their leaders have nothing to measure with and are likened to cutting off a Hydra’s head.
Socrates is said to retain the character of an unwearied and disinterested seeker after truth.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 575-666
occurrences.motif_label: Allegorical cave as image of knowledge
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly identifies the figure of the cave as a recapitulation of divisions of knowledge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The cave recapitulates divisions of knowledge; the composite animal allegorizes parts of the soul; the captain, ship, and true pilot figure the relation of people and philosophers.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 575-666
occurrences.motif_label: Ship and pilot as political-philosophical allegory
occurrences.basis: The noble captain, ship, and true pilot are described as a figure for the relation of the people to philosophers in the State.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The cave recapitulates divisions of knowledge; the composite animal allegorizes parts of the soul; the captain, ship, and true pilot figure the relation of people and philosophers.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5775-5855
occurrences.motif_label: celestial order governed by Necessity and time powers
occurrences.basis: Necessity, her daughters, and the Sirens coordinate the celestial circles and the temporal sequence of past, present, and future.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The spindle turns on Necessity's knees; a Siren sings on each circle; Lachesis, Clotho, and Atropos sit on thrones and sing of past, present, and future.
Clotho guides the outer circle with her right hand, Atropos guides the inner circles with her left, and Lachesis guides both in turn.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5775-5855
occurrences.motif_label: choice of next life by lot and moral discernment
occurrences.basis: Souls receive lots, view possible lives, and are warned that wise understanding is needed to choose well and avoid evil.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “A new period of mortal life has begun”; souls may choose, and “the responsibility of choosing is with you—God is blameless.”
The interpreter casts lots among the souls, each takes the lot near him, and many more samples of lives than souls are laid before them.
The samples include human and animal lives, tyrannies ending in misery and exile, famous lives of men and women, and mixed conditions of wealth, poverty, sickness, and health.
The passage states that education should teach refusal of evil, choice of good, knowledge of life's combinations, and selection of the life that makes the soul better.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5857-5941
occurrences.motif_label: saved tale as moral salvation through knowledge and justice
occurrences.basis: The narrator says the saved tale will be salvation if hearers believe in the immortal soul and hold to Justice and Knowledge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The narrator addresses Glaucon: the saved tale will be salvation if hearers believe in the immortal soul, follow Justice and Knowledge, pass undefiled over Forgetfulness, and receive reward and happiness.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 5943-6033
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom through philosophical abstraction
occurrences.basis: Plato is presented as convincing people of the fallibility of sense and opinion and the reality of abstract ideas.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Plato rejoices in banishing poets, associates them with inferior faculties, treats Homer and Hesiod as no rule of life, and is described as opposing poetry to philosophy, sense to abstract ideas.

The passage says Scripture opposes seen to unseen things and that Plato similarly opposes particulars of sense to universals and ideas; it then critiques Plato's treatment of particulars and universals.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 6123-6207
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom through rightly ordered poetry
occurrences.basis: The passage imagines poetry that expresses divine perfection, truth, justice, insight into human nature, and service to humanity.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage imagines poetry as a hymn of divine perfection, renewing the world’s youth, preserving the good, and joining love with knowledge and service.
Named poets and traditions are evaluated: Greek tragedians, Milton, Wordsworth, Hebrew prophets and psalmists, Shakespeare, Homer, Goethe, and Mephistopheles in Faust.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 6123-6207
occurrences.motif_label: Beauty guiding the soul toward reason
occurrences.basis: The passage quotes or paraphrases Plato’s idea that beauty may imperceptibly draw the soul from childhood into harmony with reason.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Plato is said not to seriously expel poets but to protest poetic unreality; readers may become what they read; beauty is compared to a breeze drawing the soul toward reason.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 6284-6350
occurrences.motif_label: choice of fate or life-lot
occurrences.basis: Lots determine order, but the passage emphasizes choosing wisely and names Odysseus as a last chooser who can still choose well.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The order of lots indicates chance, but adverse chance may be overcome by wisdom and right choice; Odysseus is cited as choosing last; habit must be joined to knowledge or philosophy.
“The freedom of the will to refuse the evil and to choose the good is distinctly asserted.” The passage also describes an open space within the walls of necessity.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 63-163
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom through philosophical method
occurrences.basis: The passage emphasizes Plato's conception of a method of knowledge and the development of major forms of thought in the Republic.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Plato is described as conceiving a method of knowledge; analyses of Socrates and Plato are said to underlie later logic and psychology, and many forms of thought are said to be found in the Republic.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 6419-6504
occurrences.motif_label: Rule by wisdom or philosopher-ruler
occurrences.basis: The ideal polity is said to come into being when a king's son becomes a philosopher, and the passage rejects a vulgar earthly reign of philosophers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage describes Plato's ideal state as impossible in his age yet retained as a pattern; it mentions the philosopher son of a king, the noble lie of earth-born men, and the Republic as a vision only.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 6506-6592
occurrences.motif_label: Ideal city or perfect state beyond existing politics
occurrences.basis: The passage presents Plato's ideal State as a philosophical response to defective existing governments and compares it with other city-oriented visions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Niebuhr asks whether Plato was a good citizen; the passage says Plato was not loyal to Athenian democracy or any existing government, regarded existing governments as factions, and judged tyranny the worst.

The decline of Athenian politics is described as the likely motive for Plato's ideal State; the Republic is compared with Augustine's City of God and with first Christians looking forward to a heavenly city.
The perfect State is called paradoxical by ordinary notions; modern readers have mocked or denounced Plato's paradoxes, but the passage argues that such thoughts deserve careful consideration.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 6594-6666
occurrences.motif_label: Philosophical vision of a higher social order
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts the practical statesman with the philosopher who can imagine distant possibilities and the influence of abstract ideas on politics.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The practical statesman sees these reflections as visionary; the philosopher sees them as possible and can imagine common property becoming as fixed as private property, asking whether the end may revert to the beginning.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 6668-6744
occurrences.motif_label: liberation from ignorance through criticism and education
occurrences.basis: The passage describes custom and ignorance as a former tyranny, tradition as a veil pierced by criticism, and education as a rapidly multiplying force.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says custom and ignorance no longer hold the world fast, criticism has pierced tradition, progress may accelerate, and education moves like a wheel with ever-multiplying rapidity.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 6668-6744
occurrences.motif_label: meeting of East and West in a common human stock
occurrences.basis: The passage says East and West may meet and all nations may contribute thoughts and experience to the common stock of humanity.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage speculates that natural science, fertility, machinery, physiology, health, peace, leisure, locomotion, crises of mind, and the meeting of East and West may contribute to humanity's common stock.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 668-755
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom inquiry through definition and refutation
occurrences.basis: Socrates asks what justice is and tests proposed answers through examples, analogies, and contradictions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates asks what justice means, whether it is telling truth and paying debts, and gives the example of returning a borrowed sword to a friend who has gone mad.
Socrates asks what Simonides meant; Polemarchus explains that justice means doing what is proper: good to friends and harm to enemies, including alliances with one and war against the other.
Socrates examines justice in peace, contracts, money keeping, attack and defense, guarding and stealing; the argument invokes Autolycus, a Homeric hero excellent in theft and perjury.
The argument asks whether friends and enemies are real or seeming, whether good should be done to the good and evil to the evil, and concludes that no sage or poet said the just return evil for evil.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 6746-6822
occurrences.motif_label: Contested wisdom across moral horizons
occurrences.basis: The passage notes the wonder that one of the wisest and best men could hold moral ideas wholly at variance with modern views.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “The first wave having been passed, we proceed to the second—community of wives and children. ‘Is it possible? Is it desirable?’”

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 6824-6912
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom as moral and rational governance
occurrences.basis: The passage emphasizes mind, reason, duty, conscience, truth, and moral judgment as necessary guides for human life and marriage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage questions placing life on a physical basis, prioritizes the moral, human, and rational, and says mind, reason, duty, conscience, truth, and mental health cannot be excluded.

The passage says Plato separated body and mind in marriage, contradicted his idealism, opposed the family sentiment of Hellas, may have been misled by Sparta, and would make one family from all families by selecting the finest men and women for breeding.

The passage expands objections to Platonic marriage, asserting monogamy as law of God and nature and citing polygamy, unequal unions, introduced vice, dynastic degeneration, marriages of convenience, inbreeding, and prostitution as evidence in sexual relations.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 6914-6987
occurrences.motif_label: Destabilizing knowledge during moral transition
occurrences.basis: The passage says anthropological speculation can unsettle older beliefs and warns that uncertainty of knowledge may excuse passion or weaken moral principle.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Speculations are unsettling because marriage may appear to be historical growth rather than revelation from heaven; nevertheless marriage and family are said to have become more defined and consecrated, with comparisons among the East, Greeks, Romans, and Christian nations.
"There is more reason for maintaining the sacredness of the marriage tie"; the passage warns that in transition from old to new beliefs people may let go of moral principle.

Some contemporary persons, influenced by anthropology or novelty, are described as believing that self-assertion of women, rebellious children, analysis of relations, or circumstances may break or relax family ties; they point to societies in America and elsewhere.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 6989-7077
occurrences.motif_label: critique of artificial selection of human excellence
occurrences.basis: The passage rejects proposed schemes of marriage lots and breeding for strength, beauty, or genius, emphasizing limits of knowledge about heredity and character.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage says nature has hidden her secret and mocks the idea that suitable marriage arrangements or Plato's system of lots could produce a Shakespeare or Milton.

The passage questions whether breeding for bulldog-like tenacity or Spartan courage would improve the world; it names Tyrtaeus, Aesop, and Newton as people who would have been exposed at Sparta, and rejects Platonic devices for pairing strong and fair persons or dissimilar natures.

The passage says people inherit mental and physical qualities from parents, remote ancestors, race, and general human conditions, but that these cannot be precisely defined or estimated and form only a small part of each individual.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7079-7146
occurrences.motif_label: suppressed sparks of exceptional genius
occurrences.basis: The passage describes remarkable individuals as sources of civic progress and criticizes systems that extinguish seeds or sparks of genius and character.

evidence.quote_or_summary: "scattered seeds or sparks of genius and character" are said to be smothered and extinguished by the criticized system.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7148-7231
occurrences.motif_label: Reason and self-restraint against passion
occurrences.basis: The passage contrasts sentimental or impulsive attachment with reason, duty, watchfulness, and self-restraint.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage invokes reason against sentimentalism and reports that Dr. Combe resisted marriage because of hereditary consumption.
A friend wore a black ribbon on his wrist to remind himself not to yield to affection because of liability to insanity; he died unmarried in an asylum.

The first rising flood of youthful passions is difficult to regulate and is stimulated by imagination; those charged with youth may mitigate harm through watchfulness, affection, example, hints, and admonitions.
The passage urges reticence and self-restraint in counsel, warning against premature disclosure, undue power, and demanding confession of evil.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7233-7307
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom as qualification for rule
occurrences.basis: The passage centers on the doctrine that political healing requires kings to become philosophers or philosophers to become kings, with philosophers defined by apprehension of the idea of good.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “Until kings are philosophers or philosophers are kings, cities will never cease from ill”; philosophers are those capable of apprehending ideas, especially the idea of good.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7233-7307
occurrences.motif_label: Initiatory second education into contemplation
occurrences.basis: Older soldiers enter a second novitiate of study and contemplation, and guardians undergo a second education toward higher knowledge and legislation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: War and philosophy are the permitted interests; when citizens are too old to be soldiers, they retire from active life to a second novitiate of study and contemplation.
The second education is directed toward higher knowledge and aims to make already good citizens into good legislators.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7233-7307
occurrences.motif_label: Contemplative vision of totality
occurrences.basis: The passage praises the intellectual condition of striving toward higher conceptions and cites the image of being spectator of all time and all existence.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A great metaphysical conception is said to ravish the mind with prophetic consciousness, and metaphysical enquirers are said not to fairly criticize their own speculations.
“He is the spectator of all time and of all existence!”

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7309-7390
occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom as qualification for rule
occurrences.basis: The passage links contemplation of the good, speculative power, and philosophical reflection with legislation and statesmanship.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Hebrew prophet is said to believe faith in God enables governance, while the Greek philosopher imagines contemplation of the good makes a legislator; both find repose in divine perfection.
The passage asks whether the ruler or statesman should be a philosopher and states that some figures have united command with thought and reflection.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7392-7476
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom through lifelong and post-life education
occurrences.basis: Plato is described as making education comprehend the whole of life and prepare for another life where education begins again.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Plato’s education begins with the Greek curriculum, extends to after-life, comprehends the whole of life, and prepares for another life in which education begins again; this is called a continuous thread through the Republic.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7478-7558
occurrences.motif_label: education as inner illumination
occurrences.basis: The passage describes knowledge as elicited from within and education as turning the soul’s eye toward light.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Knowledge is to be elicited from within; education is “not as the filling of a vessel, but as the turning the eye of the soul towards the light.”

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7478-7558
occurrences.motif_label: moral purification of inherited mythology
occurrences.basis: The passage says old mythology is to be reformed by excluding divine immoralities, underworld terrors, and bad heroic examples from youth education.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Plato would reform old mythology; Homer and Hesiod are treated as authorities for his purposes; divine lusts and treacheries, underworld terrors, and heroic misbehavior are excluded, while Homer may still teach endurance.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7478-7558
occurrences.motif_label: protective formation of youth in a purified environment
occurrences.basis: The young are to be raised away from harmful sights and sounds in a healthy atmosphere, gradually learning temperance, endurance, and balanced bodily and mental development.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The young are to grow up in happy, healthy surroundings, away from sights or sounds harmful to character or taste, with impressions of truth and goodness wafted to them.
Education is harmonious growth, teaching temperance and endurance while body and mind develop in equal proportions; simplicity is the rule of life.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7478-7558
occurrences.motif_label: divinity defined by truth and goodness
occurrences.basis: The passage states that religion is to be based on the principles that God is true and good.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Religion is based on two principles: “first, that God is true; secondly, that he is good.”

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7560-7638
occurrences.motif_label: education as preventive wisdom
occurrences.basis: The passage presents education as the means that will prevent civic disorders and take care of the rest.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Medicine is paralleled by law; greater matters are assigned to the legislator or oracle of Delphi, lesser matters to citizens; state diseases are likened to hydra heads; prevention through education is named as the true remedy.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7560-7638
occurrences.motif_label: whole-person healing
occurrences.basis: The passage states that the eye cannot be cured without the body, nor the body without the mind, and criticizes medicine that loses sight of the human frame as a whole.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Gymnastic leads to medicine, which is compared with law; medicine is criticized for complicating disease, losing sight of the human frame as a whole, and neglecting conditions of health including air and water.

According to the passage, Plato holds that “the eye cannot be cured without the rest of the body, nor the body without the mind,” and warm baths may benefit the rustic more than a doctor's prescriptions.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7560-7638
occurrences.motif_label: oracle as authority for greater matters
occurrences.basis: Greater legal matters are said to be determined by the legislator or the oracle of Delphi.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Medicine is paralleled by law; greater matters are assigned to the legislator or oracle of Delphi, lesser matters to citizens; state diseases are likened to hydra heads; prevention through education is named as the true remedy.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 757-835
occurrences.motif_label: dialectical search for wisdom through questioning inherited maxims
occurrences.basis: The passage emphasizes the interrogation of moral ideas, the setting aside of poetic authority, and the replacement of simple maxims about justice with philosophical examination.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Aphoristic morality is called inadequate; poetic authority is set aside through the 'winding mazes of dialectic'; a Persian mystic poet’s words to the Divine being are compared with Plato in relation to punishment by evil and forgiveness of injuries.

The passage contrasts definitions of justice as speaking truth and paying debts, and as doing good to friends and harm to enemies; it notes casuistry, interrogation of moral ideas, appeal to Homer, and the conclusion that the latter maxim is erroneous.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7640-7706
occurrences.motif_label: ascent toward higher truth
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly describes a movement toward perfect truth, with all things ascending to the good and reposing there.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “the good which is the higher sphere of dialectic, is the perfect truth to which all things ascend, and in which they finally repose.”

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7640-7706
occurrences.motif_label: wisdom through disciplined training
occurrences.basis: The passage presents higher education as cultivating abstraction through mathematics and dialectic in pursuit of knowledge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The passage states that true knowledge, for Plato, concerns abstractions and universals rather than particulars, individuals, poetry, or sensible beauties, and that education aims to cultivate abstraction.
“This is to be acquired through the study of the mathematical sciences. They alone are capable of giving ideas of relation, and of arousing the dormant energies of thought.”
“The dialectician is as much above the mathematician as the mathematician is above the ordinary man.”
“the good which is the higher sphere of dialectic, is the perfect truth to which all things ascend, and in which they finally repose.”

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7640-7706
occurrences.motif_label: ordering chaos through knowledge
occurrences.basis: Mathematics is described as the measure by which the chaos of particulars is reduced to rule and order.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “the only measure by which the chaos of particulars could be reduced to rule and order.”

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7708-7783
occurrences.motif_label: staged initiation toward higher knowledge or beauty
occurrences.basis: The passage explicitly says beauty in the Symposium is attained by stages of initiation and the good by regular gradations of knowledge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Idea of good is represented in the Symposium as beauty and is supposed to be attained there by stages of initiation, as here by regular gradations of knowledge.

occurrences.passage_locator: The Republic / THE REPUBLIC / INTRODUCTION AND ANALYSIS.; lines 7708-7783
occurrences.motif_label: dialectical passage beyond appearances to first principle
occurrences.basis: Dialectic is described as piercing the veil of hypotheses and reaching the final cause or first principle of all.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Dialectic is described as piercing the veil of hypotheses and reaching the final cause or first principle of all.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Socrates and Polemarchus agree that the good cannot harm anyone and that injuring a friend or anyone else is the act of the unjust, not the just; the debt formula of justice is rejected as untrue.

Socrates and Polemarchus say they will oppose attributing the rejected saying to Simonides, Bias, Pittacus, or another wise man or seer; Socrates instead suggests Periander, Perdiccas, Xerxes, Ismenias the Theban, or another rich and mighty man as possible source.

Thrasymachus roars at the company, calls their conduct folly, demands that Socrates answer as well as ask, and rejects answers such as duty, advantage, profit, gain, or interest unless there is clarity and accuracy.

Socrates says he was panic-stricken and trembling, then compares their search for justice to seeking gold, calling justice more precious than many pieces of gold and asking for pity rather than anger.

occurrences.motif_label: Wisdom contrasted with ignorance in moral argument

evidence.quote_or_summary: The speaker says he is amazed that Thrasymachus classes injustice with wisdom and virtue, and observes that Thrasymachus attributes to the unjust qualities previously attributed to the just.

The speaker introduces the arts and asks whether a musician, in tightening and loosening lyre strings, would seek to exceed another musician; Thrasymachus says he would not, though he would exceed the non-musician.

The speaker generalizes to knowledge and ignorance: the knowledgeable person would not wish to say or do more than another knowledgeable person in the same case, while the ignorant person would desire more than both the knowing and the ignorant.
The exchange concludes that the wise and good will not desire to gain more than their like but more than their opposite, whereas the bad and ignorant will desire more than both.

occurrences.basis: The passage emphasizes autumn leaf loss, winter barrenness until spring, year-round greenness, snowfall, and later crop-bearing; seasonal leaf loss protects the Fig-tree from snow damage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: “You ... lose your leaves every autumn, and are bare till the spring: whereas I ... remain green and flourishing all the year round.”

occurrences.motif_label: reserved harvest portion for a field or crop spirit
occurrences.basis: Multiple cited customs reserve a portion of the crop for named beings, sometimes explicitly in return for blessing or to secure kindness and abundance in the next year.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In a village of the Tilsit district, the last sheaf was left standing in the field for the Old Rye-woman.
In Neftenbach, the first three ears of corn reaped are thrown away on the field to satisfy the Corn-mother and make the next year's crop abundant.
In Thuringia, a little heap of after-grass is left in the field for the Little Wood-woman in return for the blessing she has bestowed.
At Kupferberg, Bavaria, some corn is left standing and dedicated to the Old Woman, with words asking that next year she be as kind as she has been this time.

In Russia, an unreaped patch of corn is left and the ears are knotted together; this is called the plaiting of the beard of Volos, is treated as tabooed, and is believed to harm anyone who meddles with it.
In north-east Scotland a few stalks were sometimes left unreaped for the benefit of the aul' man; the note says this is probably equivalent to the German Old Man.

occurrences.motif_label: human sacrifice for agricultural fertility and protection
occurrences.basis: The victim's flesh is buried in fields or offered to the Earth Goddess, ashes are spread on fields and mixed with new corn, and the passage links the victim's tears with rain.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Other reported killing methods include dragging the victim through fields in Chinna Kimedy while flesh is cut away, fastening him to a revolving wooden elephant, and exposing him on a sloping stage to fire and hot brands so that his tears would correspond to abundant rain.

Flesh cut from the victim is carried rapidly to villages; those at home fast until it arrives. The priest divides it, buries one portion for the Earth Goddess with water poured from a hill gourd, and household heads bury portions wrapped in leaves in fields.

In some places flesh is hung on a pole by the stream watering the fields. Three-day restrictions may follow. Remaining head, bowels, and bones are watched, burned with a sheep, and ashes are scattered on fields, applied to houses or granaries, or mixed with new corn; some remains are buried instead.

occurrences.basis: The passage repeatedly links the victim’s body, blood, ashes, or other substances with crop growth, seed, fields, and harvest customs.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Meriah is described as partly offered to the Earth Goddess, while flesh and ashes are buried in fields, scattered over fields, placed on granaries, or mixed with new corn, implying direct crop-fertilizing power.
The author compares other sacrifices: Marimo ashes scattered over fields, a Brahman lad’s blood put on crop and field, and a Sioux girl’s blood allowed to trickle on seed.
The author states that fertilizing virtue appears both in mixing victim’s blood or ashes with seed-corn and in the European custom of mixing grain from the last sheaf with young corn in spring.

The passage says victims were identified with corn through physical correspondence: Mexican young or old victims for young or ripe corn, Marimo short and fat victims as seed, Pawnee fattening, and killing or grinding victims like corn.

occurrences.motif_label: Slain representative of the corn-spirit
occurrences.basis: The representative of the corn-spirit is described as annually killed on the harvest-field, with variants involving strangers, last harvesters, masters, and Lityerses.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Frazer says human beings have been killed to promote crop growth; he argues that the Lityerses story and European harvest customs indicate that a representative of the corn-spirit was annually killed on the harvest-field in Phrygia and Europe.
Passing strangers are described as manifestations of the corn-spirit escaping from cut or threshed corn, and as being seized and slain.

The corn-spirit is said to lurk in the corn, retreat before harvesters, and be expelled from the last corn, sheaf, or grain; the nearest reaper, binder, or thresher is then treated as the corn-spirit.

Frazer says Lityerses was himself slain, probably wrapped in a corn-sheaf, beheaded, and cast into the river; modern harvest customs often perform a pretence of killing on the master, farmer, or squire.

occurrences.basis: Attis and Lityerses are treated as vegetation figures whose personal representatives were annually slain, with seasonal distinction between spring and harvest rites.

evidence.quote_or_summary: At Pessinus, the high-priest appears to have been annually slain in the character of Attis, a vegetation god; Attis is described as a reaped ear of corn and possibly identical with Lityerses as a corn-spirit embodiment.

Frazer warns that the same people may have distinct vegetation deities with representatives slain at different seasons; he compares spring tree-spirit and autumn corn-spirit rites and distinguishes Attis as especially a tree-god from Lityerses as harvest-linked.

Attis and Lityerses are described as parallel vegetation spirits or deities whose personal representatives were annually slain; Attis became a state religion, while Lityerses remained a rustic Phrygian harvest-field rite, possibly involving a human victim for the corn-spirit.

Frazer compares this with Mexico, where a human harvest victim was crushed between stones, and with India and Africa, where victims' ashes were scattered over fields; he cautions that the Harrân legend may simply express grinding corn and scattering seed.
